abstract.p: Streptococcus mutans is a major contributor to dental caries, and its biofilm formation is associated with treatment challenges. Therefore, identifying medicinal plants and natural compounds with antibacterial and anti-biofilm activities is important for the development of new therapeutic approaches. This study aimed to investigate the antibacterial and anti-biofilm effects of honey, aqueous extracts of sumac and Miswak fruit, royal jelly, lactogum, and silver diamine fluoride (SDF) against S. mutans. The antibacterial effects of the compounds and extracts were evaluated using a well diffusion assay. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) was determined by broth microdilution. Biofilm formation was quantified using the crystal violet assay, and metabolic activity was assessed by the MTT assay. Morphology of the biofilms was examined by scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Additionally, the expression of key genes involved in biofilm formation (gtfB, gtfC, and gtfD) was measured by RT-PCR. The findings indicated that the antibacterial effects of honey, Miswak aqueous extract, sumac fruit extract, and SDF were comparable to chlorhexidine. MICs were 512 mg/mL for honey, 512 mg/mL for sumac fruit extract, 512 mg/mL for royal jelly, and lactogum, with Miswak aqueous extract and SDF showing MICs of 256 mg/mL and 32 mg/mL, respectively. SDF, Miswak aqueous extract, and sumac fruit extract exhibited the strongest anti-biofilm effects, down-regulating gtfB, gtfC, and gtfD expression in S. mutans biofilms. Collectively, these results suggest that honey, Miswak and sumac aqueous extracts, and SDF have notable antibacterial activity against S. mutans and can inhibit biofilm formation through downregulation of gtfB, gtfC, and gtfD.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Dental caries is a common infectious disease caused by bacterial colonization that leads to decalcification of the inorganic portion of the tooth and is accompanied by substantial degradation of the organic matrix1. Evidence suggests that mutans group streptococci play a major role in the initiation and progression of the disease2. Consequently, many therapeutic approaches—such as antibacterial chemical agents, fluoride therapy, and antibiotic therapy—aim to reduce this bacterial group in the dental flora. Although multiple factors influence the development and progression of dental caries, acidogenic bacteria—especially Streptococcus mutans biofilms—play a pivotal role in its development3. S. mutans is a Gram-positive, facultative anaerobic, non-motile bacterium with the ability to metabolize various sugars, including sucrose, which lowers tooth pH, leads to enamel dissolution, and contributes to the appearance of caries symptoms4. The ability of this bacterium to form biofilms depends on the presence of the enzyme glucan sucrase/glucosyltransferase (a member of the glycoside hydrolase enzyme family, GH70), encoded by the gtf gene5. Therefore, inhibition of this gene can prevent biofilm formation, and drugs that suppress the expression of this gene may be considered as therapeutic and preventive options for dental caries5.

Recently, medicinal plants and their natural products have attracted attention for the treatment of infectious diseases, including dental caries. For example, Gloria-Garza et al. (2025) cataloged medicinal plants and their extracts with protective effects in the treatment of dental caries and showed that flavonoids, polyphenols, and essential oils present in medicinal plants can contribute to oral hygiene and caries prevention by exerting antibacterial and anti-inflammatory effects6. Another study demonstrated that methanolic extracts of the medicinal plants Syzygium aromaticum, Nigella sativa, and Psidium guajava exhibited strong antibacterial effects against caries-causing agents, including S. mutans7. Similarly, honey has gained attention as a potent antibacterial agent in infectious diseases such as dental caries; in vitro studies have shown that honey can inhibit the growth of S. mutans, indicating its potential for prevention and treatment8. Furthermore, royal jelly combined with honey showed the highest antimicrobial activity against dental caries–causing bacteria Fusobacterium nucleatum and Porphyromonas gingivalis, while S. sobrinus and S. pyogenes displayed relatively high resistance to royal jelly and honey9. Salvadora persica (Miswak) has been used in oral hygiene since ancient times and, because of its bioactive compounds, exhibits a wide range of pharmacological activities, including anticancer, anti-inflammatory, lipid-lowering, antidiabetic, sedative, and antimicrobial effects10. For example, extracts from this plant demonstrated inhibitory effects against strains isolated from children’s dental plaque11. Similarly, Sumac fruit (Rhus coriaria L.) has shown potential for use in the prevention and treatment of dental caries. The aqueous extract of the fruit inhibited Streptococcus sorbinus with MIC and MBC values of 0.390 mg/mL and 1.5 mg/mL, respectively, and reduced biofilm formation by S. mutans by 86.1%12. Analysis of the essential oil of Sumac revealed that β-caryophyllene (20.2%) and cembrene (11.1%) were the most dominant constituents, which may underlie the antimicrobial activity of Sumac fruit13. However, comparative studies of the antimicrobial activities of the aforementioned natural compounds and medicinal plants are scarce in the literature. Accordingly, the present study aims to investigate the antimicrobial activity of natural products and medicinal plants—such as honey, royal jelly, Miswak (Salvadora persica) skin and adjacent wood, Sumac fruit—as well as commercial products such as Lactogum and silver diamine fluoride—against S. mutans.

sec.title: Preparation of S. mutans
Natural products and medicinal plant extracts
sec.p: Natural, unpasteurized and untreated honey obtained from bees feeding with wild plant blossoms was obtained from beekeepers in Isfahan, Iran. Honey was dissolved in sterile saline at different concentrations (w/v) to be used in subsequent experiments. Dragee supplement containing Royal jelly was obtained from the Kooze Asal Company, Isfahan Province, Iran and its different concentrations were prepared by dissolving royal dragee in distilled water. It is worth noting that the main chemical constituents of royal jelly include carbohydrates (primarily glucose and fructose), royal jelly proteins, lipids (primarily 10-HDA), and water. This natural substance produced by honey bees also contains notable amounts of minerals, vitamins, and other bioactive compounds14. Sumac fruit (R. coriaria) and S. persica (Miswak) were obtained from the Pharmacognosy Department of the Faculty of Pharmacy, Isfahan University of Medical Sciences. We used fresh outer bark and adjacent wood of the Miswak tree, collected from healthy stems, to prepare the extract. 20 g of dried plants were ground into powder by a grinder, 200 ml of distilled water was added, and boiled for 10 min. After boiling the plant-water mixture for 10 min, the mixture was allowed to cool briefly, then it was filtered to remove plant debris. The filtrate was placed in a bain-marie and evaporated under gentle, controlled heat until the volume was reduced to approximately one-fifth of the original volume (until a paste-like consistency suitable for further processing), ensuring the temperature did not exceed 60–70 °C. The resulting extract was stored at 4 °C until use. The bain-marie setup was maintained with gentle agitation to prevent scorching. Silver diamine fluoride was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Corp. (USA, CAS no# 7681-11-0). Lactogum was obtained from Zist-Takhmir Company (Tehran, Iran) containing 109 CFU of Streptococcus salivarius strains.

sec.title: Antibacterial activities
sec.p: The antibacterial effects of aqueous extracts of Miswak tree (prepared from outer bark and adjacent wood) and sumac fruit, as well as honey, royal jelly, lactogum and silver diamine fluoride were investigated using the well diffusion method. For this purpose, S. mutans cultured in BHI agar medium plates were used. A hole was created in the culture medium using a sterile pipette and different concentrations of each of the above-mentioned substances were poured in each well. The well containing dimethyl sulfoxide liquid as a negative control. The plates were placed at 37 °C for an overnight and then the diameter of growth inhibition zone was measured using a caliper.

sec.title: MIC and MBC
sec.p: 200 µL of 512, 256, 128, 64, and 32 mg/mL of each of the extracts and compounds used in the present study were added to each well of a 96-well plate in BHI broth. Then, 20 µL of bacterial suspension (half McFarland) was added to each well. Also, wells containing S. mutans and culture medium were considered as positive and negative controls, respectively. The plates were incubated for 24 h at 37 °C. In the next step, 50 µL of triphenyltetrazolium chloride was added to each well and incubated for 3 h. The first concentration of the substances in which no red color was formed was considered as the MIC concentration. To measure MBC, 10 µl of the contents of the wells without red color were transferred to BHI agar medium and incubated for 24 h. The lowest concentration of the material at which no bacterial growth was observed was considered as the MBC concentration.

sec.title: Biofilm formation and metabolic activity
sec.p: The MIC concentrations of the extracts and natural products used in the study were poured into the microplate and then half McFarland equivalent of S. mutans was added. The microplates were incubated for 4 and 24 h at 37 °C under anaerobic conditions. After incubation, the microplates were washed three times with sterile PBS and fixed with methyl alcohol for 15 min. At this stage, 100 µL of crystal violet was added to the wells and kept at room temperature for 10 min and washed again three times with PBS. Finally, 100 µL of 95% ethanol was added and the OD was read at a wavelength of 550 nm. Chlorhexidine was considered as a positive control and the well with bacteria and no treatment was considered as a negative control. We also studied the effect of the extracts and natural products used in this research on biofilm of S. mutans by scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
After formation, the metabolic activity of the biofilm was measured by adding 100 µL of MTT solution, incubating the microplates in the dark for 3 h, and reading the OD at 590 nm.

sec.title: Hydrophobic surface and bacterial aggregation measurement
sec.p: To measure the hydrophobic surface, different concentrations of S. mutans were incubated anaerobically at 37 °C for 0 and 30 min. Then, the microtubes were centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 5 min, washed with sterile PBS buffer, and the OD was recorded at 550 nm.

To measure the aggregation rate, S. mutans was first incubated overnight in BHI broth at 37 °C under anaerobic conditions and then centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 30 s. After washing with PBS, the OD was read at 600 nm. Then, the same was done by treating S. mutans with extracts and natural products at MIC concentrations and the OD was read at 600 nm again. The percentage of bacterial aggregation was calculated from the difference in the OD readings.

sec.title: Gene expression measurements
sec.p: RNA extraction from S. mutans treated with MICs of extracts and natural products used in the present study was performed using a commercial RNA extraction kit (Parstous, Iran) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The quantity and quality of extracted RNA were assessed by NanoDrop and gel electrophoresis, respectively. After ensuring the quantity and quality, cDNA was synthesized from extracted RNA using a commercial cDNA synthesis kit (Parstous, Iran). The primer sequences of gtfB, gtfC and gtfD genes were designed by Primer 3 software and blasted on the NCBI website. After ensuring the accuracy of the sequences, primers were synthesized. The primer sequences of the studied genes are given in Table 1.

caption.p: The primer sequences of gtfB, gtfC and gtfD genes.

sec.p: The RT-PCR reaction mixture consisted of 5 µL of Cybergreen, 0.5 µL of each of the reverse and forward primers, 3.5 µL of sterile double-distilled water and 1 µL of cDNA in a final volume of 10 µL. The time-temperature program of the device consisted of one cycle of 95 °C for 10 s, 30 cycles of 95 °C for 10 s, 60 °C for 10 s and 72 °C for 20 s.

sec.title: Cytotoxic evaluation assay
sec.p: In the present study, we used MG-63 cells (Prepared by the Pasteur Institute of Iran, ATCC Number: CRL-1427) to investigate the cytotoxic effects of some natural products and medicinal plants used in this study. For this purpose, cells (105 cells) were added to each well of a 96-well plate. Then, different concentrations of treatments (64 to 512 mg/ml) were serially added into each well. Also, positive control (untreated cells) and negative control (treatments only) were considered. After treating the cells for 24 h, the cells were washed three times with phosphate buffer solution (PBS) and 20 µL of MTT solution was added to each well and incubated for 4 h in the dark. Finally, 100 µL of DMSO solution was added to the wells and after 15 min, OD was read at wavelengths of 490 nm.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All data analyzed in GraphPad Prism software via ANOVA procedure and Tukey’s test (Significant level: P < 0.05).

sec.title: Antibacterial activity
sec.p: We evaluated the antibacterial effects of honey, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and sumac fruit, royal jelly, lactogum, and SDF against S. mutans in a well diffusion assay using chlorhexidine as a control, and the results are presented in Table 2; Fig. 1. As can be seen, the mean diameter of the zone inhibition of honey (31.33 ± 1.52 mm), Miswak tree extract (29.67 ± 1.52 mm), and SDF (32.00 ± 2.00 mm) against S. mutans were comparable to the chlorhexidine (31.67 ± 1.52 mm), indicating the strong antibacterial effects of these compounds and extracts against this dental infection pathogen. However, the diameter of the zone inhibitions observed for royal jelly and lactogum were smaller compared to the aforementioned compounds and extracts (Table 2). Statistical analysis indicated that the diameter of the inhibition zone for royal jelly (P < 0.001) and lactogum (P < 0.0001) was significantly lower than that of chlorhexidine, and no significant difference was observed in the diameter of the inhibition zone of other compounds and extracts with chlorhexidine (Fig. 1), indicating that honey, Miswak tree and sumac fruit extracts, and SDF have antibacterial effects equivalent to chlorhexidine.

caption.p: The antibacterial effects of honey, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and sumac fruit, royal jelly, lactogum, and SDF against S. mutans measured by the mean diameter of growth inhibition zone (mm). ****P < 0.0001, ***P < 0.001 compared with chlorhexidine.
The diameter of growth inhibition zone of honey, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and sumac fruit, royal jelly, lactogum, and SDF against S. mutans.

sec.title: MIC and MBC
sec.p: The MICs of the compounds and extracts used in the present study against S. mutans were measured using the broth microdilution method and the results are given in Table 3. As can be seen, the MICs of honey, sumac fruit extract, royal jelly and lactogum against S. mutans were measured to be 512 mg/mL, and the MIC of Miswak tree extract (prepared from outer bark and adjacent wood) was measured to be 256 mg/mL and the MIC of SDF was measured to be 32 mg/mL.

caption.p: The minimum inhibition concentrations (MICs) of honey, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and sumac fruit, royal jelly, lactogum, and SDF against S. mutans.

table-wrap-foot.p: Values in bold showed the MICs.
The data are OD measured by spectrophotometer.

sec.title: Biofilm formation and metabolic activity
sec.p: SDF, sumac fruit extract and lactogum had the strongest anti-biofilm effects against S. mutans, respectively, and the anti-biofilm activity of these compounds increased with increasing concentration. Among the compounds used in this study, SDF caused the greatest inhibition of biofilm formation in S. mutans, and sumac fruit extract at a concentration of 64 mg/mL showed strong biofilm inhibitory effects. However, honey (512 mg/mL), Miswak tree extract (256 mg/mL) and royal jelly (512 mg/mL) inhibited biofilm formation in S. mutans at high concentrations (Table 4). Similarly, sumac fruit extract and SDF reduced significantly metabolic activity of biofilm of S. mutans compared other compounds, indicating their strong anti-biofilm activities (Table 4).

caption.p: The anti-biofilm and metabolic activities of honey, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and sumac fruit, royal jelly, lactogum, and SDF against S. mutans.

sec.p: In addition to our quantitative assessments, we examined S. mutans biofilms by scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Representative SEM images are presented in Fig. 2. Visual inspection revealed that all tested compounds reduced biofilm coverage relative to the untreated control and disrupted the extracellular biofilm matrix. Notably, treatment with SDF, Miswak, and Sumac fruit extracts produced more pronounced disruption of the biofilm architecture and clearer signs of matrix degradation, such as thinning and breaks in the extracellular polymeric substance, compared with Royal jelly and lactogum (which showed comparatively milder effects). These observations suggest differential anti-biofilm activity among the compounds, with SDF, Miswak, and Sumac fruit extracts exerting stronger effects on both biofilm integrity and matrix integrity.

caption.p: Inhibition of biofilm formation by honey, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree (prepared from outer bark and adjacent wood) and sumac fruit, royal jelly, lactogum, and SDF against S. mutans under scanning electron microscopy.

sec.title: Hydrophobic surface and bacterial aggregation measurements
sec.p: The hydrophobic surfaces and aggregation rates of bacteria exposed to different concentrations of honey, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and sumac fruit, royal jelly, lactogum, and SDF were measured and the results are given in Table 5. As can be seen, both hydrophobic surfaces and aggregation of S. mutans increased with increasing concentrations of treatments. The lowest hydrophobic surfaces were measured in bacteria treated with aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and lactogum, and similarly, the lowest aggregation rates were observed in bacteria treated with royal jelly and sumac fruit extract. However, the highest hydrophobic surfaces and aggregation rates were measured in S. mutans treated with aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and SDF (Table 5).

caption.p: The hydrophobicity level and aggregation of S. mutans under honey, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and sumac fruit, royal jelly, lactogum, and SDF treatments.

sec.title: Gene expressions
sec.p: We evaluated the expression of gtfB, gtfC and gtfD genes in S. mutans treated with MICs of the compounds and extracts used in the present study and the results are shown in Fig. 3. As can be seen, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and sumac fruit as well as SDF significantly reduced the expression of all three studied genes compared to the control (untreated S. mutans). However, SDF showed the strongest inhibitory effects on the expression of gtfB, gtfC and gtfD genes compared to the other treatments used in this study. Furthermore, honey was able to significantly reduce only the expression of gtfC gene compared to the control (Fig. 3b).

caption.p: The expressions of gtfB (a). gtfC (b) and gtfD (c) genes in S. mutans treated with MICs concentrations of honey, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and sumac fruit, royal jelly, lactogum, and SDF.

sec.title: Cytotoxic assay
sec.p: The results of MTT assays showed that honey, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree ((prepared from outer bark and adjacent wood) and sumac fruit, royal jelly and lactogum had no cytotoxic effects on MG-63 cell line at the concentrations used (64–512 mg/mL). However, 128, 256 and 512 mg/mL of SDF reduced MG-63 cell viability almost 10%, 16% and 20%, respectively (Fig. 4).

caption.p: The effects of different concentrations of honey, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and sumac fruit, royal jelly, lactogum, and SDF on cell viability of MG-63 cell line (n = 3).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The results of the present study showed that honey, aqueous extracts of the Miswak tree and sumac fruit, and SDF had antibacterial effects against S. mutans that were comparable to chlorhexidine. Although the antibacterial effects of royal jelly and lactogum were statistically lower than chlorhexidine, both compounds were able to reduce S. mutans growth. Additionally, the MICs of honey, sumac fruit extract, royal jelly, and lactogum against S. mutans were 512 mg/mL, while the MICs of Miswak tree extract and SDF were 256 mg/mL and 32 mg/mL, respectively. This finding indicates that SDF has the strongest antibacterial effect against S. mutans, followed by the aqueous extract of the Miswak tree. Importantly, SDF, as well as the aqueous extract of sumac and lactogum, strongly inhibited biofilm formation and metabolic activity in S. mutans, indicating robust anti-biofilm effects, which was corroborated by SEM. Decreases in hydrophobicity and bacterial aggregation were observed upon exposure to these treatments. Finally, exposure of S. mutans to the aqueous extracts of the Miswak tree and sumac fruit, as well as to SDF, was associated with downregulation of genes involved in biofilm formation (gtfB, gtfC, and gtfD).

Streptococcus mutans is a major etiological factor in dental caries and imposes a substantial economic burden on patients15. Treatment approaches include antibiotic therapy, which carries the risk of antimicrobial resistance. Therefore, identifying novel treatments that do not promote resistance is of great importance. Medicinal plants and natural compounds with antibacterial properties are among these alternatives16. Accordingly, this study investigated the antibacterial effects of aqueous extracts of the Miswak tree and sumac fruit, as well as compounds such as honey, royal jelly, lactogum, and SDF against S. mutans. In the initial step, the antibacterial effects of these extracts and compounds were assessed using the well diffusion assay, and the results indicated strong antibacterial activity for honey, aqueous extracts of the Miswak tree and sumac fruit, and SDF against S. mutans.

Numerous studies have reported antimicrobial effects of honey, and aqueous extracts of the Miswak tree and sumac fruit against a broad spectrum of pathogens, consistent with the present findings. For example, Nassar et al. (2012) demonstrated that honey at 12.5% and 25% concentrations reduced S. mutans growth and inhibited biofilm formation17. Similarly, a mouthwash prepared from sumac fruit extract inhibited the growth of oral pathogens, suggesting potential as an alternative to chemical chlorhexidine mouthwash18. Moreover, Miswak has shown inhibitory effects against oral pathogens such as Lactobacillus acidophilus, S. mutans, and Porphyromonas gingivalis19. Notably, a study reported that SDF inhibited the growth and biofilm formation of S. mutans on dentine surfaces and markedly reduced dentine demineralization20. The findings of the present study align with these reports, showing that SDF and the aqueous Miswak extract exhibit stronger antibacterial effects against S. mutans than honey, royal jelly, lactogum, and the aqueous extract of sumac fruit. However, the observed cytotoxic effects of SDF on MG-63 cells, as confirmed by the MTT assay, indicate that caution is warranted in the use of this product, whereas the Miswak aqueous extract shows substantial potential for combating dental caries caused by S. mutans.

Biofilm formation on tooth surfaces by oral pathogens such as S. mutans can contribute to the initiation and progression of caries3. Biofilm formation is regulated by gtf genes, including gtfB, gtfC, and gtfD; the first two are responsible for the production of water-insoluble glucans, while gtfD synthesizes water-soluble glucans5. Glucan formation is associated with a biofilm matrix that enhances bacterial survival and complicates infection treatment. Consequently, in this study, the effect of all tested compounds and extracts at their MIC concentrations on the expression of gtfB, gtfC, and gtfD was evaluated. The results indicated that exposure of S. mutans to the Miswak and sumac aqueous extracts, as well as SDF, downregulated gtfB, gtfC, and gtfD expression, which could underlie their anti-biofilm effects. Notably, Vahid-Dastjerdi et al. (2016) also reported that aqueous sumac extract inhibited the expression of gtfB, gtfC, and gtfD in S. mutans, consistent with the present findings21. Additionally, Takahashi et al. (2021) showed that exposure of S. mutans to SDF inhibited biofilm formation, aligning with the current results22. In the present study, SDF exhibited the strongest anti-biofilm effect among the tested compounds and extracts. It is worth to mention that the observed downregulation of biofilm-associated genes gtfB, gtfC, and gtfD upon exposure to aqueous Miswak extract, sumac fruit extract, and SDF points toward a molecular mechanism wherein these agents interfere with glucosyltransferase-mediated synthesis of extracellular polysaccharides, a key determinant of biofilm architecture and adherence23. Additionally, reductions in bacterial hydrophobicity and aggregation imply alterations in cell surface properties and intercellular cohesion, which could further diminish colonization efficiency24. Collectively, the data support a multi-targeted mode of action: direct bactericidal or bacteriostatic effects, impairment of biofilm matrix formation, and modulation of cell-surface characteristics. Such combined effects are desirable in caries prevention strategies, where disruption of early biofilm establishment can have lasting impacts on oral health outcomes.

The present study contributes to the growing body of evidence that natural products can rival conventional antiseptics in mitigating the growth and virulence of S. mutans, a primary etiological agent of dental caries. The observed antibacterial effects of honey, aqueous extracts of the Miswak tree, and sumac fruit, as well as SDF, were comparable to chlorhexidine in inhibiting S. mutans proliferation. Although royal jelly and lactogum exhibited statistically weaker antibacterial activity than chlorhexidine, their capacity to reduce bacterial growth nonetheless indicates potential utility as adjunctive antimicrobial agents, particularly in populations seeking less synthetic intervention.

While the in vitro findings are compelling, caution is warranted when extrapolating to clinical settings. Factors such as salivary flow, buffering capacity, pH dynamics, and the presence of polymicrobial communities can influence efficacy and safety. Standardization of extract preparations are essential to ensure reproducibility and dose optimization. The comparable efficacy of SDF to chlorhexidine is particularly noteworthy, given SDF’s additional anti-caries effects and ease of use in pediatric populations, though concerns about esthetics and patient acceptance warrant consideration. For future work, in vivo studies and randomized clinical trials should evaluate not only antibacterial and anti-biofilm outcomes but also caries incidence and lesion progression over time. In this study, we used MD-63 (human osteosarcoma) cells to assess the cytotoxic effects of the compounds and extracts. This cell line is a robust in vitro model with high reproducibility and relatively low biological variability, making it particularly suitable for initial cytotoxic screening of dental biomaterials and natural extracts. However, to understand the effects of these natural compounds and extracts within the dental environment, studies should extend to additional oral-relevant cell lines. To capture the full biological complexity of the oral milieu, the next logical step is to employ cell lines more specific to soft oral tissues, such as Human Gingival Fibroblasts (HGF) or Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OSCC) lines. Furthermore, investigations into synergistic combinations—such as SDF with Miswak extract or sumac—could reveal additive or synergistic effects that lower required concentrations and reduce adverse events. Finally, exploring molecular pathways—beyond gtfB/C/D expression, including microbial interactions and host response—would deepen understanding of how these natural agents influence the complex ecology of the oral microbiome.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Overall, it is concluded that honey, aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and sumac fruit, as well as SDF have strong antibacterial effects against S. mutans. It was also found that aqueous extracts of Miswak tree and SDF can prevent biofilm formation in S. mutans and the mechanism of action of these anti-biofilm effects seems to be the downregulation of the gtfB, gtfC, and gtfD genes. However, given the cytotoxic effects of SDF on MG-63 cells, the aqueous extract of the Miswak tree appears to be a safer option.
